title: Planning Meals on a Budget
instructions: Listen carefully. Choose the option that best matches what is said or implied.

audio.description: Friends discuss a low-cost meal plan and what to buy.

transcript.text: We have spent too much on lunches this month. I do not want to prepare every meal, but we could cook soup Sunday and freeze a few portions.
I will bring leftover vegetables after checking they are fresh. We need filling food for nights we are out late.
We could add beans and keep bread frozen. Then we can eat quickly instead of buying food on the way home.
Let’s compare prices at both shops. The market can be cheaper, but not if we buy more than we can use.
Choose two meals first, then buy what is missing. We can share extras instead of wasting them.

questions.prompt: Why are the friends discussing a new meal plan?
options: They have spent too much on lunches.
They are hosting a large dinner.
They want to stop eating vegetables.
questions.explanation: Friend A says they have spent more than planned on lunches this month.

questions.prompt: What does Friend B want the meals to include?
questions.explanation: Friend B asks for something filling on days they are out late.

questions.prompt: Why do they plan to compare two shops?
options: One shop is only open on Sundays.
Prices vary, and buying too much could waste food.
They need to return a kitchen appliance.
questions.explanation: They say one shop may be cheaper for vegetables, but only if they do not buy more than they can use.

questions.prompt: What is their main approach to shopping?
options: Buy a large amount of everything
Plan meals first and buy only missing items
questions.explanation: They agree to choose two meals and then buy only what they are missing.
